setupSteps: Common range 30–45 degrees. Most coaching sources use 30–45 degrees; some blogs suggest 15–30. Many gym benches have notches rather than degree markings; the angle is hard to read, so use a phone level app or ask staff which notch is which.

What the research says (summary). Rodríguez-Ridao et al. 2020 (30 trained adults, 60% of 1RM, angles 0, 15, 30, 45, 60 degrees) found the upper pectoralis peaked at 30 degrees, middle and lower pectoralis were highest at 0, and the anterior deltoid was highest at 60. Trebs et al. 2010 (15 men, 70% of 1RM, 0, 28, 44, 56 degrees) found the clavicular head more active at 44 degrees than at 0 or 28 degrees, with the sternocostal head more active flat and the front deltoid more active on inclines. Chernov et al. 2025 (20 men, 20, 32 and 43 degrees) found the clavicular head at 20 degrees lower than at 32 and 43, with no significant difference between 32 and 43. Lauver et al. 2016 (0, 30, 45, minus 15) found some higher activation at 30 or 45 at certain time points, with mixed results.

FitPlate choice. Start at about 30 degrees (est.; lower shoulder load than steeper settings and clearly above flat). Move toward about 40–45 degrees once the pattern is smooth, if your shoulders are comfortable. Avoid going much above 45: the front shoulder takes over (Rodríguez-Ridao 2020). A hard medical cut-off angle is Not found.

Choose a stable bench with uprights (or a power rack with the bench inside). Check it does not wobble. If the bench has no safety arms or pins, do not train near failure alone; use dumbbells or a Smith machine (Gym 14) instead.

Set the J-hooks. Lie back and reach up; you should lift the bar off with your elbows still slightly bent. One guide suggests setting a safety bar height 1–2 inches (about 2.5–5 cm) below the lowest point of the bar's travel; apply this to the upper-chest touch point.
Set safeties just below the bar's lowest point (the touch point on your upper chest); both sides equal. Safeties matter only if set before the lift.
Eyes under the bar, then take the five points of contact below. On a steep bench the unrack can pull you off the bench, so a hand-off from a spotter is helpful.
Load evenly, same plates both sides, use collars when training with a spotter or safeties.

Pick a pair you can control for 8–10 reps. Lift the dumbbells to your thighs sitting on the bench: lighter than you think for the first session, because getting them into position is part of the lift.
Check the bench is stable and will not tip when you kick up.
Five points of contact: back of the head, upper back and shoulders, glutes, and both feet on the floor. On an incline bench your head and back rest against the pad.
Feet flat, under or slightly behind the knees. If the floor is too far for your feet, place plates or a low block under them (one source suggests this).
Shoulder blades back and down before gripping (same cue as Gym 20), keep them pinned during the set.
Grip (barbell): slightly wider than shoulder width, thumbs around the bar, wrists straight and stacked over the forearms, bar low in the palm (as in Gym 20).
Grip (dumbbell): palms forward (neutral or slightly turned in is also used), wrists straight above the elbows, dumbbells over the shoulder joints at the top.

Dumbbell kick-up (one at a time): sit on the bench with the dumbbells resting on your thighs near the hip, back against the pad. One at a time, kick the knee up to push the dumbbell to chest height, then bring it into position with your hands; do the other side. Many gyms use this method (seen as a search summary); it is more risky with heavy weights, so practise with light dumbbells and ask a spotter or staff for a hand-off for anything heavier. Check the bench will not tip.
Spotter note: ask for a spotter (section 9) and agree the hand-off and rep count before you start.

steps.title: Lie down in position
steps.action: Sit on the bench, lie back, set the five points of contact, eyes under the bar.
steps.feel: Head, upper back and glutes pressed into the bench; feet pressing the floor.
steps.visualCheck: Side: head, upper back, glutes on the bench; feet flat. Behind the head: eyes under the bar, bar centred.

steps.title: Grip and retract
steps.action: Take the grip (thumbs around), pull the shoulder blades back and down, squeeze the bar.
steps.feel: Chest lifted slightly; shoulder blades pinned; wrists straight.
steps.visualCheck: Side: forearms near vertical; wrists straight. Front: hands even.

steps.title: Unrack (with a hand-off if you have a spotter)
steps.action: Straighten the elbows to lift the bar off the hooks and move it over your shoulder joints (not your face), stop with arms straight.
steps.feel: Weight settles over the shoulders; upper back stays tight.
steps.breathing: Breathe in, do not hold long.
steps.visualCheck: Side: bar above the upper chest or shoulder joints; elbows soft.

steps.title: Lower the bar
steps.action: Bend the elbows and lower the bar in a slow, controlled path to the upper chest.
steps.feel: Upper chest stretching; upper back tight.
steps.visualCheck: Side: forearms near vertical; elbows about 45–75 degrees from the torso (est., see section 5).

steps.title: Touch the upper chest
steps.action: Lightly touch the bar to the upper chest (below the collarbone, above the nipple line, from coaching sources); no bounce.
steps.visualCheck: Side: bar touches the upper chest, not the neck or front of the shoulders.

steps.title: Press up
steps.action: Push the floor away with your feet and press the bar up and slightly back until your arms are straight and the bar is over your shoulders.
steps.breathing: Breathe out gently as you pass the hardest point.
steps.visualCheck: Side: bar travels from the upper chest up to over the shoulder joint; hips stay down.

steps.title: Lock out softly
steps.action: Finish with straight but not forced elbows over the shoulder joints.
steps.feel: Weight held by the bones in line.
steps.breathing: Finish exhaling, breathe in for the next rep.
steps.visualCheck: Side: bar above the shoulder joints. Front: arms even.

steps.title: Re-rack
steps.action: After the last rep, press the bar back until it touches the uprights, lower it into the hooks and check both sides.

steps.title: Sit and set the dumbbells on your thighs
steps.action: Sit on the angled bench with the dumbbells on your thighs near your hips, back against the pad.
steps.feel: Weight on the thighs; back supported.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back flat on the pad, feet flat.

steps.title: Kick up the first dumbbell
steps.action: Lean back; kick the knee of one leg up so the dumbbell goes to chest height, and steady it with your hand.
steps.visualCheck: Side: dumbbell at upper-chest height, elbow bent, other foot on the floor.

steps.title: Kick up the second dumbbell
steps.action: Repeat on the other side, then lie back fully with both dumbbells at chest height.
steps.feel: Both dumbbells held at the sides of the upper chest.

steps.title: Retract and press to the start
steps.action: Pull the shoulder blades back and down, and press the dumbbells up until arms are straight over the shoulder joints.
steps.breathing: Breathe in at the bottom, out on the press.
steps.visualCheck: Side: arms vertical; dumbbells over the shoulder joints. Front: even.

steps.title: Lower the dumbbells
steps.action: Bend the elbows and lower both dumbbells slowly to the sides of the upper chest.
steps.feel: Stretch across the upper chest; wrists straight.
steps.visualCheck: Side: forearms near vertical; elbows about 45–75 degrees from the torso (est.). Front: elbows not flared to 90 degrees.

steps.title: Pause briefly
steps.action: Pause with the dumbbells near the upper chest, about level with the chest.
steps.visualCheck: Dumbbells at about chest level, not below the shoulders.

steps.title: Press up
steps.action: Press both dumbbells up until arms are straight, slightly in toward each other.
steps.visualCheck: Dumbbells finish over the shoulder joints.

steps.title: Finish the set and bring the dumbbells down
steps.action: After the last rep, with arms straight, lower the dumbbells to the thighs (or to your sides) one at a time, then sit up. Do not drop them. If you cannot finish the last rep, lower under control and ask a spotter to take them; avoid dropping a dumbbell on yourself.
steps.visualCheck: Side: dumbbells rest on the thighs before you sit up.

commonMistakes.title: Bench set too steep (above about 45 degrees)
commonMistakes.text: Bench set too steep (above about 45 degrees). Why: turns the move into more of a shoulder press and the front shoulder takes over (Rodríguez-Ridao 2020). Fix: use about 30–45 degrees.

commonMistakes.title: Touching the bar to the neck, or lowering too high or too low
commonMistakes.text: Touching the bar to the neck, or lowering too high or too low. Why: bar near the throat or too low (flat-bench path) loses the point of the incline and is unsafe. Fix: touch the upper chest (below the collarbone), forearms vertical.

commonMistakes.title: Elbows flared to 90 degrees
commonMistakes.text: Elbows flared to 90 degrees. Why: sources link it to more shoulder stress. Fix: elbows about 45–75 degrees (est.).

commonMistakes.title: Sliding down the bench or lifting the hips
commonMistakes.text: Sliding down the bench or lifting the hips. Why: the angle changes, the lower back arches, and the bar path shifts. Fix: lighter weight, feet planted, glutes and back on the pad.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping dumbbells after the set
commonMistakes.text: Dropping dumbbells after the set. Why: a jerky end is hard on the rotator cuff and can injure you or others. Fix: lower to the thighs under control, or ask a spotter to take them.

commonMistakes.title: Kicking up weights that are too heavy
commonMistakes.text: Kicking up weights that are too heavy. Why: loss of control before the first rep. Fix: use lighter dumbbells for the kick-up, or ask a spotter for a hand-off.

commonMistakes.title: Thumbless grip (barbell)
commonMistakes.text: Thumbless grip (barbell). Why: the bar can slip from the palm. Fix: thumbs around the bar.

commonMistakes.title: Bouncing the bar or dumbbells at the bottom
commonMistakes.text: Bouncing the bar or dumbbells at the bottom. Why: loses control and loads the joint. Fix: 3 seconds down, light touch or short pause.

commonMistakes.title: Loose shoulder blades
commonMistakes.text: Loose shoulder blades. Why: the shoulder joint takes the load. Fix: retract before you start and keep them pinned.

commonMistakes.title: Ego loading and no safeties
commonMistakes.text: Ego loading and no safeties. Why: the bar can trap you; incline presses are weaker than flat presses (est.). Fix: start light, use safeties or dumbbells.

safetyNotes: Shoulder problems: the incline shifts load to the front of the shoulder; use a lower angle (about 30 degrees), dumbbells with a neutral grip, a lighter load or a machine press, and ask a professional.
Wrist or elbow pain: use dumbbells with a neutral grip; stop if pain rises.
High blood pressure: the breath-hold (Valsalva manoeuvre) raises blood pressure; breathe out on each push, avoid sets to failure, keep loads moderate.
Pregnancy: an incline bench avoids lying flat on the back but ask your obstetrician (see table).
Recent surgery, osteoporosis, heart disease: see the table; ask a professional.

Do you need one? Yes for anything near hard effort and for your first sessions. A spotter's biggest help is the lift-off and the re-rack (barbell) or the dumbbell hand-off. With the empty bar or light dumbbells and safeties set, a spotter is optional but still sensible for a beginner. A CSCS-style study guide lists 2–3 spotters for an incline press, versus 1 for dumbbells.
How to ask: ask gym staff or a trainer first. Say it before the set: "Could you spot me on the incline? I will do 8 reps. Please give me a hand-off, and only touch the bar if I ask."

Barbell hand-off: you lie back, grip, retract, and say "ready". The spotter lifts the bar off the hooks with you and lets go once it is over your shoulder joints. After your last rep say "take it" and the spotter helps guide the bar back to the hooks.
Dumbbell hand-off: the spotter hands you each dumbbell at chest height (or you kick up at light weights). At the end the spotter takes the dumbbells from your wrists, one side at a time.
During the set: the spotter stands at the head of the bench, hands close but not on the weights, and follows the path. If you stall, say "help".

When training alone: use dumbbells at a weight you can lower to your thighs under control, or use the barbell only in a rack with safety arms or pins set just below your upper-chest touch point; stop 3 reps before failure. If you cannot set safeties, use dumbbells, a Smith machine (Gym 14) or a chest press machine (Gym 22) instead. Never roll a barbell down your body.

Bail-out: barbell: lower the bar to your chest, rest it on the safeties and slide out. Dumbbells: lower them to your chest and thighs under control; avoid dropping them toward your head or body (if you must dump them, drop them to the sides, away from you, and be careful; seen as a coaching tip only).
